what_its_for: Meropenem is an antibiotic used to fight serious bacterial infections in different parts of the body, including the lungs, stomach, skin, urinary tract, and brain (meningitis). It kills harmful bacteria so your body can recover from infection.
how_to_take: Meropenem is given as an injection directly into your vein (IV) by a nurse or doctor in a hospital or clinic. You will NOT give this medicine to yourself at home in most cases. Each dose is given slowly over 15 to 30 minutes, or sometimes over 3 to 4 hours depending on your treatment plan. Never try to inject this medicine yourself unless your healthcare team has fully trained you to do so.
dosing: Your dose will be decided by your doctor based on your age, weight, kidney function, and the type of infection you have. Common adult doses range from 500 mg to 2,000 mg (2 grams) given every 6 to 8 hours. Children's doses are based on body weight. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions. Complete the full course of treatment even if you feel better early.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given by a healthcare provider in a medical setting, a missed dose is unlikely. However, if you are receiving this medicine at home through an IV and you miss a dose, give it as soon as you remember UNLESS it is almost time for your next scheduled dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never double up on doses. Call your home health nurse or doctor if you are unsure what to do.
storage: The unopened vials of meropenem powder should be stored at room temperature, away from heat and light. Once the powder is mixed (reconstituted) into a solution, it must be used right away or stored in the refrigerator and used within the time frame your pharmacist specifies (usually within 24 hours when refrigerated). Do not freeze the mixed solution. Keep all medications out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor or pharmacist about ALL medicines you take, including over-the-counter drugs and supplements. Avoid taking valproic acid (a seizure medication such as Depakote) while on meropenem, as meropenem can make valproic acid much less effective and may put you at risk for seizures. Avoid probenecid unless your doctor approves, as it can increase meropenem levels in your body. Do not stop treatment early just because you feel better — finishing the full course helps prevent antibiotic resistance.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or seek emergency help right away if you experience: a severe allergic reaction (trouble breathing, swelling of your face, lips, tongue or throat, hives or rash); severe diarrhea or bloody stools that may occur during or after treatment (possible C. diff infection); seizures or unusual shaking; confusion, agitation, or hallucinations; signs the infection is not getting better after a few days; muscle twitching; or pain, redness, or swelling at the IV site.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within 2 to 3 days of starting meropenem, but it is very important to complete the entire course of treatment as prescribed. Stopping early, even if you feel well, can allow the infection to return and may make it harder to treat in the future.
special_populations: Kidney problems: Your doctor may reduce your dose or give doses less often if your kidneys do not work well. Make sure your doctor knows if you have kidney disease. Pregnancy: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Use only if clearly needed. Breastfeeding: Small amounts of meropenem may pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: Meropenem can be used in babies and children, with doses carefully adjusted by weight. Older adults: Kidney function tends to decline with age, so your doctor will check your kidney levels and may adjust your dose.
